The eggs of Common sole (Solea solea) contain a substantial initial energy reserve, with each fertilised ovum carrying approximately 2 J  derived from the biochemical composition of the yolk. This energy provision is calculated from the dry mass of the egg, which has been measured at 0.00012 grams , with total lipids comprising about 13.3% of the dry weight and crude proteins accounting for roughly 65.9%. Following fertilisation and embryonic development within the pelagic egg, hatching occurs after approximately 4.5 days  when incubated at a stable temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. The newly emerged prolarvae measure about 0.325 cm  in total length and possess a dry weight of roughly 51.9 micrograms , relying entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves during this lecithotrophic phase. Continued development at 13 °C leads to the onset of exogenous feeding, or age at birth, at approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days], at which point the free-swimming larvae have attained a total length of about 0.425 cm [Lb = about 0.425 cm] and a dry body mass near 91.96 micrograms  at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C].

The transition from the pelagic larval phase to the benthic juvenile stage involves a profound morphological transformation known as larval metamorphosis, which is completed when individuals reach a total length of approximately 1 cm . During this period, the larvae undergo an allometric shift and a complete body plan reorganisation, culminating in benthic settlement. The time from birth to the end of metamorphosis has been estimated at around 28 days after birth  when larvae are reared at a consistent temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. By the completion of metamorphosis, the juvenile fish have accumulated a dry weight of about 1.8 mg , representing a substantial increase in biomass from the initial feeding larva. This phase of rapid growth and development is energetically demanding, and the peak ingestion rate of food, approximated by the maximum surface-area-specific consumption of dry mussel meat, has been measured at 800 J per day per square centimeter (800 J/d.cm^2) , providing the physiological capacity to support such accelerated mass gain.

Sexual maturation in Common sole exhibits notable sexual dimorphism in both size and timing. Under thermal conditions typical for the species (13 °C [T = 13 °C]), females attain puberty at a total length of approximately 27 cm [Lp = approximately 27 cm], with a corresponding wet body mass of around 173 grams [Wwp = around 173 grams], whereas their first successful spawning event, representing the onset of reproduction, occurs at roughly 942 days after fertilisation [tR = roughly 942 days after fertilisation]. Males, by contrast, reach sexual maturity at a smaller size of about 22 cm [Lp = about 22 cm] in total length and reach first reproduction at an earlier age of approximately 708 days after fertilisation [tR = approximately 708 days after fertilisation] at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. The male's pubertal wet weight is correspondingly lower at roughly 87 grams [Wwp = roughly 87 grams]. Populations in cooler waters, such as those in the North Sea where the average temperature is approximately 10 °C [T = 10 °C], exhibit a delayed onset of reproduction, with individuals commencing spawning at about 3 years after fertilisation [tR = about 3 years after fertilisation].

Maximum body size and longevity in Solea solea also differ markedly between the sexes. Asymptotic total length for females is estimated at 48 cm [Li = 48 cm], with a corresponding ultimate wet body mass of approximately 1109.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 1109.7 grams]. Males reach a smaller asymptotic length of 42 cm [Li = 42 cm], achieving a maximum wet weight of about 701 grams [Wwi = about 701 grams]. The maximum recorded lifespan for females under natural conditions is roughly 26 years [am = roughly 26 years] at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], whereas males have a somewhat shorter maximum longevity of approximately 24 years [am = approximately 24 years] at the same temperature. Reproductive effort scales substantially with body size; a large female of 45 cm total length produces on average about 3,014 eggs per day (approximately 3013.7 eggs per day)  over the spawning season, corresponding to approximately 3,014 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 3,014 eggs per spawning event] if spawning is continuous, when the water temperature is 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. For an individual at its ultimate size, the maximum daily egg production rate rises to approximately 3,027 eggs per day, which can be expressed as roughly 3,027 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 3,027 eggs per spawning event] at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], reflecting the considerable energetic investment that iteroparous adults channel into gamete production annually.

Comparative analyses across flatfish species reveal that the life-history strategy of Solea solea is characterised by a moderately paced schedule that balances size, longevity, and reproductive output. Unlike many smaller pleuronectiforms that mature rapidly and exhibit shorter lifespans, the common sole's extended adult phase and large asymptotic size in females are consistent with a life-history pattern that prioritises repeated spawning events over several decades. The significant sexual dimorphism in both ultimate length and mass is not unusual among flatfishes, where females typically outgrow males to accommodate the volumetric demands of the ovary and the production of large numbers of pelagic eggs. Field surveys and growth-curve analyses consistently indicate that the species attains its maximum body dimensions relatively slowly, with the von Bertalanffy growth parameters reflecting a prolonged period of somatic expansion before the energetic demands of reproduction begin to dominate the energy budget of mature individuals. This combination of a large body size, a multi-year juvenile phase, and a considerable adult lifespan allows the common sole to buffer against variable recruitment success in the dynamic coastal and shelf environments it inhabits across its European range.
